extracted.intended_audience: analytic and computational number theorists; researchers interested in the Mertens conjecture and related computations
extracted.subtask_description: A concise survey of the history, computational methods, heuristic arguments, and disproofs related to the Mertens conjecture (bounds on the summatory Möbius function M(x)/√x). It covers definitions, computational formulas and sieves, the h(y,T) trigonometric proxy, lattice/L3 techniques, and effective bounds for counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Möbius function µ(n) and summatory function M(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: µ(1) = 1; µ(n) = (−1)^k if n is the product of k distinct primes; µ(n) = 0 if n is divisible by a square > 1. M(x) = sum_{1 ≤ n ≤ x} µ(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M(x) counts the difference between the number of squarefree positive integers with an even number of prime factors and those with an odd number of prime factors; correct definitions are the basis for any computation or theoretic argument about the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mertens conjecture statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjecture states that |M(x)| / √x < 1 for x > 1, where M(x) = Σ_{n≤x} µ(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central inequality investigated; numerical computations and theoretical analysis aim to verify or refute this bound and to locate counterexamples if they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness of M(x)/√x implies Riemann hypothesis and simplicity of zeros
rubrics_metrics.description: The boundedness of M(x)/√x (i.e., existence of a fixed bound for all x) implies an analytic continuation of 1/ζ(s) to ℜ(s) > 1/2, which would imply the Riemann hypothesis and that all nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) are simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by partial summation (expressing 1/ζ(s) in terms of M(x)) and analytic continuation; this implication is motivation for the conjecture and explains its strong consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Mertens-type relations to compute M(n) from smaller data (formulas (2.4) and (2.5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations expressing M(n) in terms of µ(1),…,µ(k), M(k) and M(n/2), M(n/3),…, M(n/k) with k = ⌊√n⌋ (formula (2.4)), and the alternative formula M(n)=2M(k) − Σ_{r,s≤k, rs ≤ n} µ(r)µ(s) (formula (2.5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations allow computation of M(n) for large isolated n without factoring all numbers up to n and were historically used (Mertens, von Sterneck); they also serve as consistency checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined von Sterneck relations (formula (2.6)) for computing M(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization using ω_j(n) (the count of integers ≤ n not divisible by first j primes) giving a relation that for j=0 reduces to (2.4) and for j=1,2,3,4 can reduce the range of required precomputed values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying (2.6) with higher j lets one compute M(n) from a table of M-values up to ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊n/3⌋, …, ⌊2√n⌋ for n>200, and was used by Von Sterneck and later authors to extend computed ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieve-based computation of µ(n) (Erathostenes-type sieving and vectorized sieves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute µ(n) for all n ∈ [1,N] by a sieve resembling the sieve of Eratosthenes, marking multiples of primes and squares to set µ(n)=0 or flip sign; vectorized implementations accelerate this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in systematic computations (Neubauer, Van de Lune et al.). Practical notes: vector computers and careful memory usage drastically speed up computations; this method is more efficient than factoring each n individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic/analytic proxy h(y,T) approximates M(x)/√x under RH and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define x = e^y and m(y)=M(e^y)e^{−y/2}. Theorem 3.1: under the Riemann hypothesis (all zeros ρ = 1/2 + iγ up to height T, simple), the trigonometric sum h(y,T) (explicit formula (3.9)) approximates values of m(y) arbitrarily closely and infinitely often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus to find large values of M(x)/√x it is effective to search for large values of h(y,T); h(y,T) is easier to study numerically because it is a finite trigonometric sum depending on zeros up to T and their arguments ψ_γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Kronecker-type inhomogeneous Diophantine approximation to align phases γy − ψ_γ
rubrics_metrics.description: If the γ's (imaginary parts of zeros) are linearly independent over Q, Kronecker's theorem implies there exist integers y and m_γ such that |γ y − ψ_γ − 2π m_γ| < ε for all chosen γ up to T, permitting coherent alignment of cosine terms and arbitrarily large h(y,T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a heuristic justification that h(y,T) (and hence m(y)) can be made arbitrarily large by aligning many cosine terms; practical search translates this into a lattice/approximation problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform inhomogeneous approximation into a shortest-vector lattice problem and apply the L3 algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an (n+2)×(n+2) integer-scaled lattice matrix (see matrix in (4.14)-(4.15)) with parameters α_j and scaling ν so that short vectors correspond to y making γ_j y − ψ_j − 2π m_j small; apply L3 to the lattice to find such vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key practical choices: pick α_j to weight contributions, choose ν (e.g., 2n ≤ ν ≤ 4n), include a large multiple 2^{ν} n^4 in (n+1)-st coordinate to force a unique long vector with that coordinate; Odlyzko & Te Riele used this method to find y giving large |h(y,T)| and thereby disprove Mertens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of zeros by weight |1/(ρ ζ'(ρ))|
rubrics_metrics.description: Order zeros ρ = 1/2 + iγ so that the quantities |1/(ρ ζ'(ρ))| are monotonically decreasing; select the top n zeros (e.g., n≈70) which contribute most to the h-sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerics show the first few terms dominate the sum; Odlyzko & Te Riele ordered the first 400 zeros by decreasing |1/(ρ ζ'(ρ))| and considered subsets V_n to target those with maximal contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required numerical precision and choice of T (height up to which zeros are used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computations require extremely high precision of zeros and a sufficiently large truncation parameter T (e.g., T = γ_{2000}, γ_{10000}, γ_{20000}). Odlyzko & Te Riele used ~100 decimal digits for 2000 zeros; later work used 250 digits for 10,000 zeros and 20,000 zeros for stronger records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High precision is necessary so that phase alignment (γ y − ψ_γ) and the weights are accurate; choice of T should be large enough that the finite sum in h(y,T) captures the dominant contribution of the chosen zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical parameter choices for successful lattice search (n,T,ν and target sum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic/empirical choices used: n up to about 70 (where sum of α-weighted terms exceeds 1), T equal to γ_{2000}, γ_{10000}, …, ν chosen in range (2n … 4n), and scaling of the (n+1)-th coordinate by 2^{ν} n^4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Odlyzko & Te Riele found that for n=70 and T=γ_{2000} the constructed lattice and L3 produced y with h(y,T)>1; later improvements used larger T and more zeros to increase h(y,T) and the margins by which 1 is exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective disproof criterion (Pintz-type sufficient condition via h_P(y,T))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pintz's theorem: define h_P(y,T) (modified sum with damping factors, see (5.16)). If there exists y ∈ [e^7, e^{5×10^4}] with h_P(y,T) > 1 + e^{−40} for T = 1.4×10^4, then there is some x < e^{y+√y} with |M(x)|/√x > 1 (i.e., an explicit upper bound on the smallest counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an effective route from a computed h-value to an explicit bound on x for which the Mertens conjecture fails; used by Te Riele, Kotnik, Saouter et al. to produce explicit (huge) upper bounds on the smallest counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/computational standards and resource requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale computations require careful algorithmic choices and significant computing resources (mini-computers, vector machines, Cray-1s), multiple-precision arithmetic packages (Brent's MP), and sieving/vectorization to handle ranges up to 10^{14} or more and tens of thousands of zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical notes: different teams used TI 980B, vectorized sieves, Cray-1 with MP package, and very high-precision zero computations; proper implementation and cross-checks (consistency relations like (2.4)) are essential to avoid errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative theoretical approaches (linear relations among zeros) as independent disproof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches based on studying linear relations among zeros (Bateman et al., Grosswald, Best & Trudgian) yield disproofs or bounds via different heuristics/criteria than the lattice/L3 method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods analyze the possibility of linear relations c_γ γ = 0 with constrained coefficients and use different analytic tools to produce large values of M(x)/√x or to bound lim sup/lim inf; they provide complementary evidence and may improve numerical bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and interpreting extremal/truncation results (lim sup / lim inf bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present computed lower bounds like lim sup_{x→∞} M(x)/√x ≥ 1.6383 and corresponding lim inf ≤ −1.6383, and report the best record h(y,T) values and corresponding y and T used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reported bounds are the standards by which progress is measured and should include details of T, number of zeros, numeric precision, and the computed y (with decimal digit counts) so that the community can evaluate reliability and reproducibility.
